title: Johannes Vermeer
wiki_lead:
Johannes Vermeer ( vər-MEER, vər-MAIR, Dutch: [joːˈɦɑnəs fərˈmeːr]; see below; also known as Jan Vermeer; October 1632 – 15 December 1675) was a Dutch painter who specialized in domestic interior scenes of middle-class life. He is considered one of the greatest painters of the Dutch Golden Age. During his lifetime, he was a moderately successful provincial genre painter, recognized in Delft and The Hague. He produced relatively few paintings, primarily earning his living as an art dealer. He was not wealthy; at his death, his wife was left in debt.
Vermeer worked slowly and with great care, and frequently used very expensive pigments. He is particularly renowned for making masterful use of light in his work. "Almost all his paintings", Hans Koningsberger wrote, "are apparently set in two smallish rooms in his house in Delft; they show the same furniture and decorations in various arrangements and they often portray the same people, mostly women."
The modest celebrity he enjoyed during his life gave way to obscurity after his death. He was barely mentioned in Arnold Houbraken's major source book on 17th-century Dutch painting (Grand Theatre of Dutch Painters and Women Artists, published 1718) and, as a result, was omitted from subsequent surveys of Dutch art for nearly two centuries. In the 19th century, Vermeer was rediscovered by Gustav Friedrich Waagen and Théophile Thoré-Bürger, who published an essay attributing 66 works to him, although only 34 paintings are universally attributed to him today. Since that time, Vermeer's reputation has grown enormously.

Pronunciation of name
In Dutch, Vermeer is pronounced [vərˈmeːr], and Johannes Vermeer as [joːˈɦɑnəs fərˈmeːr], with /v/ assimilating to the preceding voiceless /s/ as [f].The usual English pronunciation is  vər-MEER, with  vur-MEER, with a long first vowel, occurring in the UK.  vər-MAIR is also documented. Another pronunciation,  vair-MEER, is attested from the UK.


Life

Relatively little was known about Vermeer's life until recently. He seems to have been devoted exclusively to his art, living out his life in the city of Delft. Until the 19th century, the only sources of information were a few registers, official documents, and comments by other artists; for this reason, Thoré-Bürger named him "The Sphinx of Delft". John Michael Montias added details on the family from the city archives of Delft in his Artists and Artisans in Delft: A Socio-Economic Study of the Seventeenth Century (1982).


Youth and background
Johannes Vermeer was baptized within the Reformed Church on 31 October 1632. His Flemish mother, Digna Baltens (c. 1596–1670), was from Antwerp. Digna's father, Balthasar Geerts, or Gerrits (born in Antwerp in or around 1573), was a highly skilled metalworker, clockmaker, and coin-die cutter. A craftsman in these skills held a high social and economic status, and belonged to a highly educated elite of precision artists and mechanics. At this time, cities like Antwerp and Mechelen in Flanders were central hubs for merchants, refugees, and religious dissidents from southern Europe. Antwerp was Europe's leading global trade center, which created a unique environment for cross-fertilization between science, art, and industry. Gerrits was later arrested in Holland for counterfeiting. The family's movement from Antwerp to Amsterdam and ultimately to Delft coincides with the Flemish exodus of artisans and merchants who fled religious persecution and economic collapse in the south during the Eighty Years' War. Following the fall of Antwerp to Spanish forces in 1585, Protestants, Marranos (hidden Jews or Conversos), and Moriscos (hidden Muslims) faced intense religious persecution. The city had previously been looted and burned in 1567 by Spanish soldiers, who killed thousands of residents. grok_lead: Johannes Vermeer (1632â1675) was a Dutch Golden Age painter from Delft, widely regarded as one of the greatest painters in history. He is best known for Girl with a Pearl Earring (c. 1665) and The Milkmaid (c. 1658). Despite producing only about 34â36 authenticated works, his mastery of light, interior domestic scenes, and pointillÃ© technique make him central to Dutch art history. Born in Delft, Netherlands, he created intimate domestic interior scenes, characterized by exquisite use of light, subtle color harmonies, and precise depiction of everyday objects, often featuring women engaged in quiet activities like reading letters or pouring milk, infused with symbolic undertones. Despite his limited output, Vermeer's works commanded high prices from patrons during his lifetime, reflecting his reputation among contemporaries, though he remains one of the most enigmatic figures in art history due to scant biographical records. Vermeer was baptized on October 31, 1632, in Delft, the son of a Protestant innkeeper and art dealer, and he spent his entire life in that city. In 1653, the same year he joined the Guild of St. Luke as a master painter, he married Catharina Bolnes, a Catholic woman from a prosperous family, and converted to Catholicism to do so; the couple had fifteen children, four of whom died in infancy. His early works included history paintings and mythological subjects, such as Diana and Her Companions (c. 1655â1656), but he soon shifted to genre scenes of middle-class life, possibly influenced by artists like Pieter de Hooch and Carel Fabritius. Vermeer likely trained himself or under a local master like Leonaert Bramer, as no formal apprenticeship is documented, and he may have used a camera obscura to achieve his optical precision. Among his most iconic paintings are Girl with a Pearl Earring (c. 1665), a tronie or character study now housed in the Mauritshuis in The Hague; The Milkmaid (c. 1658â1660) at the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam, depicting a servant pouring milk in a sunlit kitchen; and View of Delft (c. 1660â1661), a rare cityscape praised for its luminous atmosphere. His style emphasized psychological depth and stillness, with figures often isolated in softly lit rooms, exploring themes of love, faith, and domestic virtueâevident in works like Woman Holding a Balance (c. 1664) and The Allegory of Faith (c. 1670â1672), the latter reflecting his Catholic conversion. Vermeer's primary patron was the affluent Delft burgomaster Pieter van Ruijven, who owned nearly half of his oeuvre, but the artist's slow production rate and the economic crisis of 1672, known as the "Disaster Year," led to financial ruin; he died insolvent in December 1675, leaving his widow to sell his art to settle debts. Rediscovered in the 19th century after centuries of obscurity, Vermeer's paintings now rank among the most valuable in the world, influencing modern artists with their timeless serenity and technical mastery. Recent scholarship, including a 2023 biography, has highlighted the profound role of Jesuit Catholicism in shaping his iconography and worldview.
